title: Amoretti 54
short: This is Sonnet 54 of Spenser's Amoretti (1595), a sequence of 89 sonnets on his courtship of Elizabeth Boyle, whom he married in 1594.
body: The Amoretti was printed in 1595 together with the Epithalamion, Spenser's marriage poem. Unlike most Petrarchan sequences, it ends in marriage, and several critics have argued that the sonnets follow the church calendar of 1594 (Lent to Easter). Sonnet 54 is one of several that complain of the lady's hardness before she accepts him. The archive keeps the 1595 spelling ('worlds', 'ydly', 'ioy', 'hart', 'sencelesse').

title: The world's theatre
short: This is the theatrum mundi, the old idea that the world is a stage on which people play parts while God or others watch.
body: The idea goes back to antiquity: the Stoic Epictetus compares life to a play in which each person acts an assigned part (Enchiridion 17). It runs through the Renaissance, in Erasmus's Praise of Folly and in Jaques's 'All the world's a stage' (As You Like It 2.7). Spenser makes it private: the world is a theatre and his love is its only audience. The usual spectator of the world's play is God, so putting the lady in that seat suggests a god-like indifference.

title: The idle spectator
short: The lady is an unmoved spectator, sitting 'ydly' (at ease, uninvolved) while the lover acts.
body: 'Ydly' (idly) means without action or care. Her leisure is set against his effort, and the picture suggests a lady of rank at a play or court entertainment. In 'we stay' (l. 1), 'stay' means dwell for a time: life on earth is a short stay. The word comes from Latin spectare, to watch, and the lady does nothing but watch. The lover plays for an audience of one, and everything in the poem depends on her response, which never comes.

title: pageants
short: 'Pageants' are scenes or shows in a play. The lover plays every part himself, a one-man show of moods.
body: A pageant was first the wagon-stage of a mystery play, then the scene acted on it, and then any show or spectacle. To 'play one's pageant' meant to act a part. 'Disguysing diversly' (l. 4) means presenting his troubled feelings in different costumes, and 'disguise' carries a sense of masquing. The plural suggests a whole festival programme. Each mood the lover shows is a new scene for the same unmoved audience.

title: mask
short: To 'mask' is to take part in a masque or masked revel, that is, to put on mirth like a costume.
body: The court masque, with its disguised dancers, was a popular entertainment. 'Mask in myrth' suggests that his joy is a performance put on for her, 'lyke to a comedy'. 'When glad occasion fits' (l. 5) means when a happy chance arises. The verb also suggests that his mirth hides his real feelings, as a mask hides a face. The lover is both actor and victim of his own moods, which change 'when glad occasion fits', so that the stage image fits a life ruled by chance and by her moods.

title: Comedy and tragedy
short: The lover's moods become the two dramatic kinds: his joy is comedy, his sorrow tragedy.
body: The octave pairs the two genres, comedy as the play of joy and tragedy as the play of woe. Renaissance readers knew this distinction from the essays on drama by Evanthius and Donatus printed with editions of Terence. The Spenserian rhyme scheme (abab bcbc cdcd ee) links each quatrain to the next, so the move from 'comedy' to 'tragedy' happens on interlocking rhymes.

title: The turn
short: This is the volta. The lady's 'constant eye' never changes, and neither comedy nor tragedy moves her.
body: 'Constant' is an ironic compliment. Constancy is the lover's virtue, but here it is the steadiness of indifference. In line 10, 'rues my smart' means pities my pain: to 'rue' is to feel sorrow for, and 'smart' is sharp pain. The 'eye' that watches without changing returns to the image of the spectator in l. 2. Where Petrarchan sonnets often turn at line 9 from complaint to resolution, here the turn shows only that the lover's whole performance has failed to touch her.

title: The perverse spectator
short: She is worse than unmoved, because she responds the wrong way: she mocks his laughter and laughs at his tears.
body: Classical theory expected an audience to feel pity and fear at tragedy (Aristotle, Poetics 13-14), and Horace says that if you want me to weep, you must first grieve yourself (Ars Poetica 102-3). A spectator who laughs at tragedy and mocks mirth breaks those expectations. Her heart that 'hardens evermore' recalls the hardening of Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 7-11).

sources.cite: Horace, Ars Poetica 101-103

title: mone
short: 'Mone' is moan, or lament. The couplet asks what can move her if neither mirth nor grief can.
body: 'Move' is the key verb of Renaissance rhetoric and poetics, which held that poetry should teach, delight and move (as in Sidney's Defence of Poesy). Judged by every art of persuasion, the lover's double performance has failed. 'Merth' and 'mone' sum up the comedy and tragedy of the octave in two alliterating words. The couplet's question then receives its own answer in the last line, a sharp ending typical of the Spenserian couplet.

sources.cite: Philip Sidney, The Defence of Poesy (1595), on poetry's power to move
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'moan, n.'

title: The senseless stone
short: A Petrarchan exaggeration: a woman whom no passion can move is not human but unfeeling stone.
body: The stony mistress is a convention that goes back to Petrarch and to Dante's rime petrose ('stony rhymes'). 'Sencelesse' means without feeling and also without understanding. Some readers see a sly hint of Pygmalion, whose statue came to life through love (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10), looking ahead to the lady's later softening in the sequence. The insult of the last line turns the theatre conceit into an image of sculpture.
